highlights.content: [Skip to Sidebar](#sidebar) [Skip to Content](#content) [![PPC Land](https://ppc.land/content/images/2026/04/PPC-Land-logo-2.png)](https://ppc.land) ![A typewriter fed by trillions of tokens of books, striking one key at a time, the way an LLM writes](/content/images/size/w2000/2026/10/llm-large-language-model-next-token-typewriter-library-explainer.jpg) A typewriter fed by trillions of tokens of books, striking one key at a time, the way an LLM writes # Explaining LLM An LLM, or large language model, is a neural network trained on vast text to predict the next token, the engine behind ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and AI search. * [![Luis Rijo](/content/images/size/w2000/2024/09/rijo.webp)](/author/luis/) by [Luis Rijo](https://ppc.land/author/luis/) [![Luis Rijo](/content/images/size/w2000/2024/09/rijo.webp)](/author/luis/) [Luis Rijo](/author/luis/) Luís Rijo has written PPC Land daily since founding it in 2016. Over 10,000 articles, funded by readers, no sponsored coverage. Tips and corrections: luis@ppc.land + [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/danielrijo) * • * 9 min read * [Share on X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F&text=Explaining%20LLM) * [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F&quote=Explaining%20LLM) * [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F&summary=Explaining%20LLM) * [Share on Pinterest](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F&description=Explaining%20LLM) * [Email](mailto:?subject=Explaining%20LLM&body=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F) A **large language model** (LLM) is a computer program that has learned to predict the next fragment of text from the fragments before it, and has been trained to do so on a body of writing so large that the prediction becomes useful for drafting, summarising, translating, coding and answering questions. It exists because a single statistical model trained on general text turned out to perform many language tasks that once each needed a purpose-built system. ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude and Meta's Llama are all LLMs, and so are the components that now sit inside search engines, ad platforms and social feeds. "Large" refers to two quantities: the number of **parameters**, the adjustable numbers inside the model that store what it has learned, and the volume of training text. Neither has an agreed threshold. A model with a few billion parameters counts as "small" today. ## How an LLM produces text The model never sees words. Text is first split into [tokens](https://ppc.land/tokens/), chunks of characters drawn from a fixed vocabulary that commonly holds 50,000 to 200,000 entries. In English, one token averages about four characters, so 100 tokens correspond to roughly 75 words, according to OpenAI's help centre. Each token is converted into a long list of numbers, an **embedding**, that places it in a mathematical space where related meanings sit close together. Those numbers then pass through a stack of identical layers built on the **transformer** architecture. The key operation is **attention**: at each layer, every token computes how much weight to give every earlier token when updating its own representation. That is how the model links "it" to a noun three sentences back. The final layer outputs a probability for every token in the vocabulary. A sampling step picks one, guided by settings such as **temperature**, where a value near zero favours the most likely token and higher values allow less likely choices. The chosen token is appended to the input and the whole process repeats, one token at a time, until the model emits a stop token or hits a length limit. That runtime process is called [inference](https://ppc.land/inference/), and it is where most of the operating cost of an LLM sits. highlights.content: OCP is extending its standards mission from servers and racks to the full AI infrastructure stack, encompassing silicon, cooling, power distribution, facilities and utility-grid integration. AMD introduced its Helion agentic AI rack, while Arm and NVIDIA outlined new CPU architectures and infrastructure requirements for rapidly expanding autonomous workloads. Meta detailed the engineering behind its Prometheus AI cluster in Ohio, including fabric structures, new optical networking, open-source transport software and AI-optimized concrete. Broadcom and NVIDIA presented advances in Ethernet networking and optical interconnects designed to overcome the growing physical constraints of accelerator clusters. New OCP data center and grid-resilience specifications, along with NVIDIA's advances in dynamic power management, signal a shift toward treating the AI factory as a coordinated, grid-aware infrastructure system. Standing before thousands of engineers and technology executives at the opening of the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose, Meta's Santosh Janardhan pointed to the enormous fabric structure surrounding the audience. It was, he explained, an example of the same construction technology Meta had begun deploying to accelerate its massive AI infrastructure buildout. At the company's Prometheus AI cluster in New Albany, Ohio, traditional assumptions about data center construction had given way to an urgent question: What if the next generation of AI infrastructure could be built in months rather than years, using engineered fabric structures instead of conventional concrete-and-steel buildings? "We are actually also training a model while we were building it," said Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure. The presentation offered a striking illustration of the larger message emerging from Monday's opening keynotes: The AI factory is becoming a fundamentally different kind of data center. Across presentations by AMD, Meta, Arm, Broadcom and NVIDIA, a common theme emerged. The rapid expansion of AI inference and autonomous agents is forcing new approaches to computing, networking, construction, power distribution and operations. At the same time, the diversity of silicon architectures and the enormous physical scale of deployments are making common infrastructure specifications increasingly important. The result is a significant expansion of OCP's original mission. Fifteen years after the organization began applying open-source principles to hardware design, the industry's next challenge is developing interoperable infrastructure across the entire data center, from processor architecture to the utility connection. OCP CEO George Tchaparian opened the summit by describing an organization whose scale increasingly reflects the industry's transformation. This year's event attracted approximately 15,000 attendees, with another 3,000 on a waitlist. Tchaparian said OCP expects membership to exceed 700 organizations by year-end, while technical contributions are growing approximately 30% annually. The organization has already announced that its 2027 Global Summit will move to San Francisco's Moscone Center to accommodate further growth. More consequential than the attendance figures, however, is the widening scope of OCP's work. Originally centered on open server designs, racks and supporting hardware, the organization's roadmap now encompasses facilities infrastructure, liquid cooling, power distribution, firmware, security, networking and the increasingly complex connections between data centers and utilities. Tchaparian characterized the emerging approach as "chip-to-grid" infrastructure. This reflects a fundamental engineering problem. As hyperscalers and AI infrastructure providers deploy increasingly specialized processors, the electrical, thermal and mechanical consequences of those design decisions extend well beyond individual servers. [Sweta Kumari](/author/sweta-kumari) New Delhi 7 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 5:06 PMIST #### Listen to This Article Microsoft has announced Maia 300, its next-generation custom [artificial intelligence](https://www.business-standard.com/technology/artificial-intelligence) (AI) chip designed to run AI models across its data centres, as technology companies seek to control the cost of operating AI services. The company plans to begin large-scale deployments of its Azure Maia systems in 2027, with the chips expected to become the primary inference platform for its products and services. Microsoft is not the only major technology company deploying custom chips for AI inference. From Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to Amazon's Trainium and OpenAI's planned inference chip, the industry is moving towards greater control over the hardware that powers AI services.   **Why inference is becoming the focus** AI computing has two broad stages: training and inference. Training involves processing large amounts of data to build a model, while inference is the process of using that trained model to generate an answer, write code, summarise a document or complete another task. As AI tools become available to more users, inference becomes a recurring operating expense. Every query, generated image, coding suggestion or interaction with an AI agent consumes computing resources. highlights.content: UPDATED 10:38 EDT / OCTOBER 13 2026 ### On theCUBE Pod: AI doubters get loud, and IBM seeks competitive advantage by Devony Hof Americans have big concerns about artificial intelligence, but that hasn’t stopped OpenAI Inc., Nvidia Corp., IBM Corp. and others from charging ahead. Last week saw shares of Nvidia, CoreWeave Inc., Oracle Corp. and Nebius Group N.V. decline amid reports that OpenAI’s annualized net revenue was approximately $50 billion, roughly $20 billion below previously reported figures. Despite the ongoing public pushback against AI, John Furrier (pictured, right), research executive analyst at theCUBE Research, sees the uproar as temporary. “This is an AI freakout moment,” he said. “It’s funny to watch knowing what’s happening on the inside. We talk to all those suppliers, whether it’s Nvidia, the chip side … the neoclouds or the AI infrastructure clouds. This new AI layer is a system; the data center as a system is now the computer. Rack scale is changing. Companies like Marvell, Broadcom and others are creating chips to create more efficiencies.” On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, left), chief analyst at theCUBE Research, discussed takeaways from the recent IBM Analyst Council. They also explored chipmaker Marvell Technology Inc.’s growth and the industry shift toward inference. ### IBM bets on commodity models Big Blue’s recent meeting provided insights into the legacy company’s position in the AI era. As Vellante sees it, customers are increasingly spending on the infrastructure and models needed to produce intelligence before turning to IBM to put that intelligence to work, presenting a challenge for the company as the AI market matures. “The alpha is going to be in your data, your processes and your operating model,” Vellante said. “This is [IBM’s] opportunity. That AI operating model is going to be the new source of competitive advantage. It’s not going to come from Palantir; it’s not going to come from models. It’s going to come from your own proprietary data, how you apply that data, how you streamline your processes and how fast you can get products and services to market.” IBM has promoted a four-part architecture composed of agents, data, automation and hybrid infrastructure, with an orchestration layer that can integrate agents from different vendors. Rather than relying exclusively on proprietary models, IBM is positioning itself as a provider of hybrid AI operating infrastructure for enterprise customers, building on Red Hat’s open-source foundation. “Their bet is the commoditization of the models,” Furrier said. “Having a nice model management capability will be good for IBM; but when you have a commoditization bet, you better be right. IBM doesn’t need its own proprietary operating system [because] … they have a valuable abstraction control layer around open infrastructure through Red Hat. Red Hat gets paid a lot of money to manage that open abstraction. That’s an opportunity: IBM could run all the agents.” The question remains whether IBM’s bet on commodity models and open-source solutions will pay off. Customers trust IBM. but they don’t see the company as an innovator in the current AI landscape, according to Vellante. However, if IBM can establish itself as a provider of the operational infrastructure around AI models and agents, then it could own “the scarcity around the abundance.” “They’ve got to play in both camps,” Vellante added. “In other words, they’ve got to have the IBM version of Oracle’s Red Stack. Last year, we asked [IBM’s CCO] Rob Thomas, what is the platform? And the answer came back: Red Hat. I agree. Let’s build a solution around Red Hat to simplify the adoption of AI. highlights.content: [![Quartz](https://static.qz.com/quartz-v1.137.0/_next/static/media/quartz-logo.1poxn91047rb6.svg?dpl=1nln7blm5540)](/) [A.I.](/tech-innovation/ai) # Intel is revealing specs for its new GPU D-series AI inference chip at industry summit The chip, formerly code-named Crescent Island, delivers 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute and 480GB of memory within a 350-watt power envelope [By Cris Tolomia](/author/cristolomia)·2 min read·Updated October 13, 2026 [Add QZ to Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=qz.com) Justin Sullivan / Getty Images Intel[$INTC](/quote/INTC) [shared technical details](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/newsroom/news/artificial-intelligence/intel-accelerates-open-infrastructure-agentic-ai-era.html) Monday on its GPU D-series AI inference chip at the Open Compute Project Global Summit, giving the product formerly code-named Crescent Island its official name and disclosing key performance specifications for the first time. According to Intel, the chip is based on the Xe3P architecture and delivers up to 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute alongside 1.5 TB/s of memory bandwidth and as much as 480GB of LPDDR5X memory, all within a 350-watt power envelope. It uses a standard PCIe form factor and air-cooled design, allowing deployment in existing data center environments without specialized rack or cooling infrastructure. Intelsaid the GPU D-series is designed for large language models, long-context workloads and concurrent inference services. A single card can support models with up to 300 billion parameters, while an eight-GPU system can handle models exceeding one trillion parameters, according to the company. "Inference is becoming the defining AI workload, and enterprises need infrastructure that delivers the right performance at the right cost," Anil Nanduri, vice president of AI Products and GTM at Intel's Data Center Group, said in a statement. "With IntelGPU D-series, we're focused on making high-capacity inference practical to deploy and economical to scale." Customer sampling of GPU D-series products is underway, Intelsaid, though the company did not announce a broad launch date or pricing. The GPU D-series targets a different performance and infrastructure profile than Nvidia[$NVDA](/quote/NVDA)'s highest-end hardware, according to [Tom's Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/intels-crescent-island-ai-accelerator-officially-powers-new-gpu-d-series-products-chip-delivers-1-3-peak-pflops-of-fp8-compute-and-1-5-tb-s-of-memory-bandwidth). Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system packs 72 Rubin GPUs, each capable of 17.5 petaflops of FP8 throughput, but the platform demands liquid cooling and draws substantially more power, according to Tom's Hardware. Intelalso introduced new Xeon-based rack designs at the summit. Select Xeon 6+ configurations can scale beyond 46,000 cores per rack at 133.45 kilowatts of total rack power, the company said. Many of the new rack designs use the Open Compute Project's Open Rack v3 standard to simplify deployment in open data center infrastructure. Intelsaid its commercialization efforts involve a range of partners across the supply chain, including OEMs, ODMs, neoclouds, independent software vendors, appliance providers, and AI-native companies. The company also highlighted a contribution to the OCP's Open Adapter Card workgroup, which is working to define a standardized sub-rack accelerator card form factor to improve interoperability across system designs. Intelhas made 116 contributions to the Open Compute Project since 2011, the company said. Daily Brief ## The essential business news, delivered fresh every morning. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/nvidia-shutterstock_2705357347-300x225.jpg) Credit: Robert Way/Shutterstock NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. **NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances** At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The [news at OCP](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/ocp-summit/) spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance. **Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP** NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. The investor verdict Microsoft’s Maia 300 announcement brings an uncomfortable question for Nvidia: what happens when a major customer starts producing more of its own AI computing? Scheduled for production deployment in 2027, the chip could strengthen Microsoft’s economics. But challenging Nvidia inside Microsoft’s services is a different task from replacing it across the AI industry. Let’s break down what Maia 300 does, how its performance claims translate into financial value and what investors should watch before declaring a winner. ## **What is Microsoft Maia 300 and when will it launch?** Maia 300 is Microsoft’s third-generation custom AI accelerator. Microsoft announced it on October 12 and plans to make the Maia family its primary inference system for its own products and services through multi-gigawatt deployments beginning in 2027. Inference means using a trained model to produce an answer or perform a task. Training builds the model’s capabilities. Inference puts those capabilities to work whenever someone asks an AI assistant to summarise a document, generate code or analyse information. | | | | --- | --- | | **Announcement detail** | **What Microsoft disclosed** | | **Announcement date** | October 12, 2026 | | **Production deployment** | Begins in 2027 | | **Main target** | AI inference | | **Intended role** | Primary inference system for Microsoft’s own products and services | | **Existing foundation** | Maia 200 already serves production workloads including Microsoft Copilot | *Sources: Microsoft’s October 12 Maia announcement; Microsoft Azure’s Maia 300 architecture disclosure.* The important word is “own”. The announcement does not establish that every external Azure customer will move to Maia. It also does not mean Microsoft is withdrawing from Nvidia hardware. Investors should distinguish an internal infrastructure decision from a market-wide migration. For[Microsoft stock](https://www.indmoney.com/us-stocks/microsoft-corporation-share-price-msft), the immediate investment question is whether running AI becomes more profitable as usage grows. Microsoft can benefit from Maia without creating a separate business selling chips to other companies. ## **Why Microsoft wants to control more of its AI costs** An AI subscription creates two financial flows. AI Agents.content: [Skip to content](#main) [Artificial Intelligence](https://gizmodo.com/tech/artificial-intelligence) # Shifting AI Doomsday Predictions Reportedly Worry Banking Regulators European regulators are expecting AI-driven financial chaos sooner than later. By [Ece Yildirim](https://gizmodo.com/author/eceyildirim) Reading time 3 minutes ![The Federal Reserve building in Washington, D.C.](https://gizmodo.com/app/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2266297470.jpg) The Federal Reserve building in Washington, D.C. © ANNABELLE GORDON / Contributor via Getty [Comments (0)](https://gizmodo.com/shifting-ai-doomsday-predictions-reportedly-worry-banking-regulators-2000825460#comments) Top financial regulators, including the Federal Reserve, are worried about American banks’ use of artificial intelligence, according to a new, anonymously-sourced report published by [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/banking-watchdogs-ramp-up-ai-scrutiny-stability-fears-mount-sources-say-2026-10-13/) on Monday. Citing “six people familiar with the matter,” Reuters reports that top banking regulators in the United States fear the increasing risks of cyberattacks, rogue AI agents, and the deployment of Chinese AI technology in the American banking system. The three regulators—the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Fed—are reportedly questioning U.S. banks, asking whether they are using AI agents to respond to cybersecurity threats and probing the kinds of guardrails the banks are establishing for safe deployment. The safeguards banks are being questioned on reportedly include whether or not the AI agents’ actions are being tracked and approved by humans, how the banks are ensuring that the agents don’t exceed authority, and whether an emergency shutdown mechanism exists if they do go rogue. Recent developments in artificial intelligence, specifically the development of supposedly encryption-ending super-hacker agent models, have caused a stir across industries, but perhaps no other sector has given more cause for concern than banking. Any AI-driven breach or malfunction that banks possibly face could jeopardize the very sensitive information, not to mention funds, of banks’ customers, including both individuals and businesses. The AI industry itself is partially driving some of this agentic AI panic, while somewhat ironically posing AI as the [best line of defense](https://industrialcyber.co/industrial-cyber-attacks/anthropic-launches-critical-infrastructure-defense-program-with-security-firms-to-protect-industrial-ot-environments/) against, well, AI. Last month, the CEO of top AI developer Anthropic, Dario Amodei, published an [essay](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier), warning that AI development was charting an unsustainable pace, and that if the industry doesn’t begin a coordinated slowdown, then humanity could face striking risks, including “serious economic disruption.” Banks themselves are also voicing security concerns related to the widening deployment of autonomous AI agents, but are [blaming external AI agents](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/13/jpmorgan-ai-agents-account-access.html) like Meta’s consumer-facing AI assistant Muse rather than any threats associated with the internal AI applications they are spending increasingly exorbitant amounts to develop and scale. Similar discussions are reportedly taking place in Europe as well. Reuters reports that top European regulators, the Bank of England and the European Central Bank, fear AI doomsday scenarios will hit financial markets sooner than expected and that banks are not up to par with their recovery plans. In fact, a senior executive at a major European bank reportedly told Reuters that they are expecting significant AI-related damage within the next six months. Recent developments in artificial intelligence, specifically the development of supposedly encryption-ending super-hacker agent models, have caused a stir across industries, but perhaps no other sector has given more cause for concern than banking. Any AI-driven breach or malfunction that banks possibly face could jeopardize the very sensitive information, not to mention funds, of banks’ customers, including both individuals and businesses. The AI industry itself is partially driving some of this agentic AI panic, while somewhat ironically posing AI as the [best line of defense](https://industrialcyber.co/industrial-cyber-attacks/anthropic-launches-critical-infrastructure-defense-program-with-security-firms-to-protect-industrial-ot-environments/) against, well, AI. Last month, the CEO of top AI developer Anthropic, Dario Amodei, published an [essay](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier), warning that AI development was charting an unsustainable pace, and that if the industry doesn’t begin a coordinated slowdown, then humanity could face striking risks, including “serious economic disruption.” Banks themselves are also voicing security concerns related to the widening deployment of autonomous AI agents, but are [blaming external AI agents](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/13/jpmorgan-ai-agents-account-access.html) like Meta’s consumer-facing AI assistant Muse rather than any threats associated with the internal AI applications they are spending increasingly exorbitant amounts to develop and scale. AI Agents.content: [Security Strategy, Plan, Budget](/topic/security-strategy-plan-budget), [AI/ML](/topic/aiml), [AI benefits/risks](/topic/ai-benefitsrisks), [Training](/topic/training) # AI hits critical mass: Prepare for a budget reckoning and security staffing surge [By Nicole Beckwith](/contributor/nicole-beckwith) ![AI agent balancing finance stacks in purple concept scene showing money scale and coin pile with smart algorithm guidance](/api/thumbor-proxy?width=1920&src=https%3A%2F%2Ffiles.cyberriskalliance.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2026%2F10%2F101326_ai_budget.jpg) (Adobe Stock Images) COMMENTARY: Cybersecurity Awareness Month is a time for enterprises to review risks, patch systems, and test backups. But for this year, it’s better to go beyond these usual tasks. For the next 12 months, expect budgets for AI to increasingly come under scrutiny, focusing on tangible ROI and what spending needs to be reined in. In the meantime, the cybersecurity threat landscape will continue to accelerate, driven by AI. According to [Mandiant’s M-Trends 2026 survey](https://complexdiscovery.com/twenty-two-seconds-to-hand-off-inside-mandiants-m-trends-2026-findings/), the median time between initial access and the handoff to a secondary threat group fell from more than eight hours in 2022 to just 22 seconds in 2025. [***SC Media Perspectives columns are written by a trusted community of SC Media cybersecurity subject matter experts.***[***Read more Perspectives here***](https://www.scworld.com/perspective)***.***] Going forward, security teams will need to have an honest conversation about the best use of AI, the risks, what the threat model is internally, and whether or not the current budget and staffing plans are going to be enough. ## AI spending faces a reckoning While AI spending is likely to remain robust, there will be more accountability for the expenditures. A key part of this is “tokenomics.”  AI agents consume large amounts of model resources, which has resulted in unexpected large bills. In some cases, enterprises have hit their annual budget limits within a few months. The [EY 2026 AI Pulse Survey](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/emerging-technologies/pulse-ai-survey) supports this. In the survey, 82% of the respondents said that they were concerned about token usage and 37% plan to re-evaluate their AI priorities and investments. A way to address the costs is to implement systems to route prompts to less expensive models, such as with harnesses. Employee training will also be critical. --- **Related reading:** * [The highest risk for AI agents is the software development organization](https://www.scworld.com/perspective/the-highest-risk-for-ai-agents-is-the-software-development-organization) * [As AI gains autonomy, who remains accountable?](https://www.scworld.com/perspective/as-ai-gains-autonomy-who-remains-accountable) * [Cybersecurity predictions that came true in the first half of 2026](https://www.scworld.com/perspective/cybersecurity-predictions-that-came-true-in-the-first-half-of-2026) --- Another factor with ROI is headcount, which is in terms of employee hours absorbed and translated into the cost of an FTE. For example, in a security operations center (SOC), AI may handle tier-1 and tier-2 alert triage while tier-3 analysts focus on more complex incidents. This can lead to consolidation of security vendors or reduction of managed services providers. Enterprise should also track metrics that measure the qualitative aspects of ROI like the false positive rate, detection coverage and analyst capacity. Finally, enterprises need to calculate the payback. AI often involves heavy upfront investments during the first couple years. So leaders need to be patient with expected returns. ## The agentic AI threat landscape is reshaping security The AI threat landscape is evolving rapidly as agents gain greater autonomy and access to enterprise systems. AI Agents.content: UPDATED 11:25 EDT / OCTOBER 13 2026 ### Workday makes Sana its new home for AI-driven HR and finance by Kyt Dotson Enterprise management software company Workday Inc. today announced that it wants to turn its existing knowledge of people, money and business rules into an operational foundation for agentic artificial intelligence tools. At Workday Rising, the company’s annual global conference, the company said Sana, an agentic experience that brings together tasks, experiences, decisions, meetings and agent activity in one place, is becoming the new Workday Home. Employees will now work directly with Sana to get everything done. The company also introduced Sana Concierge, a new service agent for human resources and information technology teams, which can resolve employee requests. It can handle onboarding, leave and password requests without passing these tedious twenty-minute tasks that can be automated to people, so they can focus on issues that require actual intuition. The company also said Sana now adapts to each employee with a “Home” experience that can tailor itself to each employee role. This includes a user interface that can generate interactive applications using Jev, a cutting-edge model from TypeSafe AI that can create forms, calendars, approval cards, visualizations and interactive experiences in real time. “AI is the new UI,” said Chief AI Officer Joel Hellermark. “Users shouldn’t have to decide which agent to use, just as they shouldn’t have to click between dozens of different systems. We’re giving our customers an agentic experience that opens up a whole new way to work.” Included in this new experience, Workday’s executives demonstrated a shift from “copilot to autopilot” during a press briefing. This follows an industry trend alongside agentic automation, where many enterprises are giving employees access to AI agents that can act behind the scenes without needing to be touched and can be triggered when data changes or comes their way, instead of needing a chat interface. For example, a recruiter autopilot agent prepares for a user’s day by checking open requisitions without waiting for the recruiter to log in, prepares outreach and surfaces candidates. Then the employee reviews outreach and chooses whether to advance candidates from the Sana interface; interview scheduling then runs autonomously. When the interview happens, the agent joins to listen in, prepare notes and uses recruiter feedback to influence future recommendations. ### Work Intelligence and Decision Intelligence As more teams begin to incorporate AI agents, models and tools, Workday announced two new platforms that help teams interact with AI experiences: Work Intelligence and Decision Intelligence. Work Intelligence helps businesses build for AI by showing enterprise teams how AI tools and agents change work. Workday said AI rarely changes a whole job at once; it can change tasks, and as those tasks change, the underlying skills that matter also change. Every worker that interacts with AI is a data point for how the company can grow. “Work Intelligence gives leaders the data to thoughtfully redesign roles, build careers and help people grow into what’s next,” said Vice President of Talent Management and Insights Nikki Helmer. Workday said it can use its deep understanding of skills, delivered through its Skills Cloud, which is now used by more than 3,450 customers and built on an ontology of more than 75,000 canonical skills, to help leadership plan how to grow people as work changes. AI won’t just change existing roles; it will create new ones too. Decision Intelligence lets HR and finance teams operate in the same space without curating and trading information across clunky communication channels, which often rely on dry reports pulled on a periodic basis. LLMs.content: [Skip to Sidebar](#sidebar) [Skip to Content](#content) [![PPC Land](https://ppc.land/content/images/2026/04/PPC-Land-logo-2.png)](https://ppc.land) ![A typewriter fed by trillions of tokens of books, striking one key at a time, the way an LLM writes](/content/images/size/w2000/2026/10/llm-large-language-model-next-token-typewriter-library-explainer.jpg) A typewriter fed by trillions of tokens of books, striking one key at a time, the way an LLM writes # Explaining LLM An LLM, or large language model, is a neural network trained on vast text to predict the next token, the engine behind ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and AI search. * [![Luis Rijo](/content/images/size/w2000/2024/09/rijo.webp)](/author/luis/) by [Luis Rijo](https://ppc.land/author/luis/) [![Luis Rijo](/content/images/size/w2000/2024/09/rijo.webp)](/author/luis/) [Luis Rijo](/author/luis/) Luís Rijo has written PPC Land daily since founding it in 2016. Over 10,000 articles, funded by readers, no sponsored coverage. Tips and corrections: luis@ppc.land + [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/danielrijo) * • * 9 min read * [Share on X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F&text=Explaining%20LLM) * [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F&quote=Explaining%20LLM) * [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F&summary=Explaining%20LLM) * [Share on Pinterest](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F&description=Explaining%20LLM) * [Email](mailto:?subject=Explaining%20LLM&body=https%3A%2F%2Fppc.land%2Fllm%2F) A **large language model** (LLM) is a computer program that has learned to predict the next fragment of text from the fragments before it, and has been trained to do so on a body of writing so large that the prediction becomes useful for drafting, summarising, translating, coding and answering questions. It exists because a single statistical model trained on general text turned out to perform many language tasks that once each needed a purpose-built system. ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude and Meta's Llama are all LLMs, and so are the components that now sit inside search engines, ad platforms and social feeds. "Large" refers to two quantities: the number of **parameters**, the adjustable numbers inside the model that store what it has learned, and the volume of training text. Neither has an agreed threshold. A model with a few billion parameters counts as "small" today. ## How an LLM produces text The model never sees words. Text is first split into [tokens](https://ppc.land/tokens/), chunks of characters drawn from a fixed vocabulary that commonly holds 50,000 to 200,000 entries. In English, one token averages about four characters, so 100 tokens correspond to roughly 75 words, according to OpenAI's help centre. Each token is converted into a long list of numbers, an **embedding**, that places it in a mathematical space where related meanings sit close together. Those numbers then pass through a stack of identical layers built on the **transformer** architecture. The key operation is **attention**: at each layer, every token computes how much weight to give every earlier token when updating its own representation. That is how the model links "it" to a noun three sentences back. The final layer outputs a probability for every token in the vocabulary. A sampling step picks one, guided by settings such as **temperature**, where a value near zero favours the most likely token and higher values allow less likely choices. The chosen token is appended to the input and the whole process repeats, one token at a time, until the model emits a stop token or hits a length limit. That runtime process is called [inference](https://ppc.land/inference/), and it is where most of the operating cost of an LLM sits. Everything the model can consider at once must fit in its **context window**, measured...

LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [AI & Machine Learning](https://shattered.io/ai-machine-learning/) # Meta’s Muse Wonder Ties Claude at 56 on AI Index [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/panand.webp) [Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/author/panand/) Updated Oct 13, 2026 · 14 min read Meta put a number on the table this week, and it is not a small one. Muse Wonder Full, the company’s newest [large language model](https://shattered.io/category/ai-machine-learning/), scored 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 exactly. The lighter Muse Wonder came in at 52, a single point behind OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra. Meta [posted the announcement](https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-wonder) on October 12, 2026, and updated the page again on October 13 as outlets including [Mashable](https://mashable.com/tech/meta-launches-muse-wonder-ai-model-family), Reuters, Quartz, Deccan Chronicle, and South Korea’s financial press picked up the story. The headline framing writing itself across tech coverage this week is that Meta has finally caught up to the two labs that have defined the frontier conversation for the past two years. The benchmark data backs part of that claim and complicates the rest. Muse Wonder Full ties or beats rivals on several measures and trails badly on at least one widely used coding test. This is a story about where Meta actually stands, not where the press release says it stands. ## What Meta Actually Announced Meta shipped two models under the Wonder name: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full. Both take text, images, audio, and video as input and return text, and both carry a context window of roughly one million tokens, enough to hold a full codebase or a lengthy research paper in a single pass. The split between the two models is about access tier, not just capability. Muse Wonder is available through the Meta Model API for any developer, while Muse Wonder Full is gated behind a Muse Code subscription. That gating matters for anyone trying to put the model through its own benchmark suite. [VentureBeat noted](https://venturebeat.com/technology/metas-new-muse-wonder-and-muse-wonder-full-models-achieve-frontier-performance-but-only-the-weaker-one-is-available-via-api) that only the weaker of the two models ships through the open API, meaning third-party developers testing Muse Wonder in production right now are not working with the same model that produced Meta’s best scores. Anyone building on top of the API should account for that gap before assuming parity with the headline numbers. The announcement also leaned on two feature names Meta is using to differentiate the release from a pure benchmark story: Active Memory, which is meant to carry context across separate conversations instead of resetting state each session, and Active Focus, designed to keep the model working through errors or dead ends and ask for permission or clarification rather than stalling out. Neither feature shows up in a leaderboard number, but both speak directly to the agentic workloads Meta is chasing with this release. ## How to Try Muse Wonder Right Now Developers can reach Muse Wonder today through the Meta Model API at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, with cached input priced at $0.20 per million tokens. Meta has set rate limits at 3,000 requests per minute and 4 million tokens per minute, limits aimed squarely at production agent workloads rather than hobbyist testing. Muse Wonder Full, the higher-scoring model, only shows up inside Muse Code for paying subscribers. Shattered.io previously covered the [pricing structure behind Muse Code’s subscription tiers](https://shattered.io/meta-muse-wonder-ai-pricing-2026/), including a top tier that had been testing at $200 a month before this launch. LLMs.content: ![]() ![Zacks](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/zacks--theme-light.svg) ![Zacks](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/zacks--theme-dark.svg) # Shopify's Biggest AI Fear Just Became Its Best Catalyst ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/meta-platforms.svg) For most of this year, the bear case on Shopify was elegantly simple. If shoppers stop browsing websites and start asking an AI agent to buy things for them, what happens to the company whose entire business is building and powering websites? Storefronts become wallpaper. Shopify becomes a commodity back end. The stock spent nine months pricing in some version of that fear. It's worth sitting with how real the concern felt. Shares ended August down 8% on the year while the S&P 500 had gained nearly 12%. For a company compounding revenue north of 30%, that gap isn't a valuation reset. That is the market quietly questioning whether the business model survives the decade. Then September happened. ![StockCharts](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/image/zacks:456cfec39094b-94fa3ed52094ebebf8f58180879d6338-resized.webp) Image Source: StockCharts ****The Meta Deal**** Back in September, Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke announced that Meta Platforms' new Muse personal AI agent would be able to complete purchases across Shopify's entire merchant network using Shop Pay. Mark Zuckerberg's framing was characteristically compact: “Shoppers find more. Shops sell more.” He added that more partnerships like it were coming soon. SHOP closed up more than 7% the following session. Two days later, Shop Pay went live as a wallet inside Muse. The detail that matters is the scope. This is not a pilot with a handful of flagship brands. It is agentic checkout across all Shopify stores. Within the same stretch, Amazon moved to block that very same agent from its marketplace. Two of the largest commerce platforms in the world looked at AI shopping agents and reached precisely opposite conclusions. One saw a threat to the customer relationship it has spent thirty years building. The other saw distribution. ****Why Shopify Gets Paid Either Way**** CFO Jeff Hoffmeister made the structural case at Goldman Sachs' Communacopia conference in September, and I'd argue it's the most important thing management has said all year. Shopify's economics do not depend on which AI assistant a shopper happens to open. Whether the journey begins in ChatGPT, in Copilot, or in Muse, if it ends at a Shopify checkout, Shopify gets paid. That single observation reframes the entire debate. Shopify isn't competing with the agents for the customer. It is becoming the settlement layer underneath them — the rails rather than the destination. Rails are a less glamorous business than storefronts. They are also a far more durable one. The behavioral data backs it up. Shoppers arriving from a large language model are 2.5 times more likely to land directly on a product page, which the company ties to roughly an 80% uplift in conversion. About 75% of AI-attributed orders in the second quarter came from outside Shopify's top 100 product categories. Agents are not cannibalizing demand that merchants already had. They are surfacing the long tail that conventional search never served particularly well. Earlier this month, Shopify extended the same logic in the other direction with Canvas, a tool that lets a merchant build a storefront by talking to Sidekick, the company's AI assistant, in roughly twenty minutes. Muse brings buyers in the front door. Canvas lowers the cost of becoming a merchant in the first place. Both ends of the funnel get cheaper at once. ****The Numbers Behind the Narrative**** Narratives are worth only what the financials support, so here is the arithmetic. Second-quarter revenue of $3.58 billion grew 34% year over year and beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 4.36%. LLMs.content: IT Brief UK - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief UK logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg) United Kingdom](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.co.uk) ![GWI expands agentic AI portfolio with new data layer](https://itbrief.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/10/14/business-analytics-dashboard-verified-data-layer-ai-assistants-story-321290.webp) [Data Analytics](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/data-analytics) [GenAI](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/generative-ai) [LLMs](https://itbrief.co.uk/tag/large-language-models) # GWI expands agentic AI portfolio with new data layer Tue, 13th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Sofiah Nichole Salivio](https://itbrief.co.uk/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNywicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--3f3cbcdb3f86206827b894ccc07566b24a1d49e6/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/unnamed%20(2).webp) SOFIAH NICHOLE SALIVIO News Editor](/author/sofiah-nichole-salivio) GWI has launched an expanded agentic AI portfolio, adding an AI intelligence layer to its product suite. The new offering lets businesses access and analyse more than 45 billion verified datapoints through existing AI platforms, including ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft Copilot, or through their own agentic infrastructure. The portfolio is designed to connect GWI's consumer attitudinal and behavioural datasets to AI assistants and agents through Model Context Protocol and the Spark API. This lets users interpret questions, identify relevant audiences and pull cited data from familiar large language model interfaces, rather than switching to a separate research platform. The update also targets different users across organisations. Non-specialists can ask questions in natural language and receive responses shaped by guided workflow prompts, while in-house analysts and data teams can predefine audiences and segments for wider use across the business. This structure is intended to keep self-service research aligned with agreed datasets and customer groups. Once an audience has been built, the system keeps conversations tied to it, applies standard filters and taxonomy to user queries, and interprets the intent behind questions to produce fuller answers. **Portfolio details** GWI has grouped the new features into three main elements: guardrails, guided workflow and intelligent tools. In practice, audience tools identify customer segments and relevant datasets, prompts help refine user intent, and the system applies a consistent framework beneath each query so repeated questions return comparable results. For businesses trying to widen access to market research while limiting inconsistency, this addresses a common issue with general-purpose AI tools. Companies often want staff outside specialist insight teams to use conversational interfaces for quick answers, while keeping those answers linked to approved definitions and source data. The latest release is aimed at both front-line teams and analysts by placing those controls inside the interfaces people already use. GWI says its underlying dataset is built from proprietary behavioural information collected over 17 years across more than 100 countries. **Commercial use** Alongside the broader portfolio, GWI has introduced an Ad-Selling Workflow for commercial and advertising sales teams. It is intended to help users produce pitch narratives based on consumer data about a client audience and its behaviour. According to GWI, client-facing teams can ask questions in natural language without needing detailed knowledge of the core GWI platform. The workflow can operate through the company's agentic products in large language models as well as in bespoke internal builds used by organisations. Science News](/images/logo-2x.png)](/) [![A service of the American Association for the Advancement of Science](/images/brand.png)](/) * [Home](/) * [News Releases](/news-releases/browse) * [Multimedia](/multimedia) * [Meetings](/meetings/announcements) * [Login](/login) * [Register](/register) News Release # Turning Foundation models into “driving mentors”: found-RL enables efficient reinforcement learning for autonomous driving [Peer-Reviewed Publication](/releaseguidelines) Tsinghua University Press [![Overall framework](https://mediasvc.eurekalert.org/Api/v1/Multimedia/76ef4d1d-e68f-44f9-85dd-aca298126e23/Rendition/low-res/Content/Public)](/multimedia/1156623) **image: Overall framework** [view more](/multimedia/1156623) Credit: Communications in Transportation Research Researchers developed Found-RL, an open-source platform that integrates vision-language models into reinforcement learning for autonomous driving. By using an asynchronous batch inference framework, Found-RL allows large foundation models to provide semantic feedback without slowing down high-frequency simulation training. Experiments in CARLA show that lightweight reinforcement learning agents can achieve competitive driving performance while maintaining real-time policy inference. The team published their study in *Communications in Transportation Research* (<https://doi.org/10.26599/COMMTR.2026.9640027>). Reinforcement learning has become a promising approach for end-to-end autonomous driving because it enables agents to learn driving policies through interaction with simulated environments. However, conventional reinforcement learning often requires extensive trial and error and may lack semantic understanding in complex traffic scenarios. Vision-language models, on the other hand, can interpret driving scenes and provide high-level reasoning, but their heavy inference cost makes them difficult to use directly in fast, multi-environment reinforcement learning loops. “Large vision-language models can provide useful driving knowledge, but directly calling them at every simulation step would make reinforcement learning training extremely slow,” says Sikai Chen, corresponding author of the study and assistant professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “Found-RL is designed to bridge this gap by allowing foundation models to guide reinforcement learning in the background, without blocking the simulation process.” **Turning foundation models into scalable driving mentors** The core of Found-RL is an asynchronous batch inference framework. Instead of waiting for a vision-language model to respond at every environment step, the platform separates simulation rollout from model inference. Multiple simulation workers send driving observations and context information to a shared request queue, while an inference server processes these requests in batches and returns feedback asynchronously. This design allows the reinforcement learning agent to continue interacting with the driving environment while the vision-language model works as a background feedback provider. The returned feedback is then matched to the correct training sample and stored in the replay buffer for learning. “Found-RL treats the vision-language model as a scalable mentor rather than a real-time controller,” Chen explains. “The lightweight reinforcement learning policy still performs high-frequency control, while the foundation model provides semantic supervision during training.” **Learning from both action guidance and semantic rewards** On top of the platform, the research team implemented two types of vision-language-model-based supervision. AI Product.content: IT Brief Australia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Australia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com.au) ![Bloomberg launches Enterprise MCP for AI data access](https://itbrief.com.au/uploads/story/2026/10/14/tony-mcmanus-story-321338.webp) [Data governance](https://itbrief.com.au/tag/data-governance) [Risk & Compliance](https://itbrief.com.au/tag/risk-compliance) [GenAI](https://itbrief.com.au/tag/generative-ai) # Bloomberg launches Enterprise MCP for AI data access Wed, 14th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.com.au/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Bloomberg has launched Enterprise Model Context Protocol, an AI access layer for its Data Licence Plus service aimed at financial institutions using AI agents with Bloomberg data. The system gives client applications a standardised way to discover, interpret and retrieve licensed Bloomberg data across more than 100 million securities and 50,000 fields. Enterprise Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is designed to address a problem that has emerged as firms test generative AI in financial services: data may be accessible, but AI systems often lack the context to understand what a figure represents, how it was calculated and whether it is suitable for a specific task. Bloomberg is packaging the service with metadata that explains fields and qualifiers such as exchange, currency, price type, period and as-of date. It is also exposing that metadata through semantic search tools, allowing agents to search for fields and instruments in natural language rather than through fixed mnemonics or manually maintained identifier lists. The service sits on top of Bloomberg's Data Licence Plus offering and brings together pricing and reference data across asset classes, company fundamentals and structure, economics and alternative data, including material from DL+ Live and the Qube Datastore. **Data context** For financial institutions, the issue is not simply pulling a number from a database. Without context, an AI system may be unable to tell which currency applies, what type of price has been provided or when the value was recorded. The aim is to let users ask for information in plain language and receive data with enough context to support research, portfolio work, risk checks and operations tasks. Bloomberg also said firms should be able to move from AI pilots to production workflows more quickly if those controls and definitions are embedded in the data retrieval process. "As generative AI adoption in financial services has grown, the bottleneck facing financial institutions has shifted from model capability to data readiness," said Tony McManus, Global Head of Enterprise Data and Indices at Bloomberg. "We've seen agents that reason well but still can't answer a basic question about a position, because the data reaching them carries no indication of what it actually represents. On its own, a last price doesn't say what currency it's in or what kind of price it is. Connections were never the hard part. Readiness is, and that's what we built Enterprise MCP to solve," said McManus. **Workflow tools** The product includes task-based tools rather than separate interfaces for each asset class. A single security discovery tool and a single field discovery tool cover the available content set. The first release also includes reusable procedures, described by Bloomberg as Skills, for point-in-time universe retrieval, corporate action adjustment and revision history. The service sits on top of Bloomberg's Data Licence Plus offering and brings together pricing and reference data across asset classes, company fundamentals and structure, economics and alternative data, including material from DL+ Live and the Qube Datastore. **Data context** For financial institutions, the issue is not simply pulling a number from a database. Without context, an AI system may be unable to tell which currency applies, what type of price has been provided or when the value was recorded. The aim is to let users ask for information in plain language and receive data with enough context to support research, portfolio work, risk checks and operations tasks. Bloomberg also said firms should be able to move from AI pilots to production workflows more quickly if those controls and definitions are embedded in the data retrieval process. "As generative AI adoption in financial services has grown, the bottleneck facing financial institutions has shifted from model capability to data readiness," said Tony McManus, Global Head of Enterprise Data and Indices at Bloomberg. "We've seen agents that reason well but still can't answer a basic question about a position, because the data reaching them carries no indication of what it actually represents. On its own, a last price doesn't say what currency it's in or what kind of price it is. Connections were never the hard part. Open Source AI.content: # 'MicroLLM lab' allows you to run seven types of ultra-compact AI models for free in your browser, and it utilizes the device's GPU via WebGPU. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/13/microllm-lab-browser-webgpu/00_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/13/microllm-lab-browser-webgpu/00.png) A free web application called 'MicroLLM lab' has been released that allows you to run seven different small AI models, including Hugging Face's 'SmolLM2' and OpenAI's 'GPT-2,' in your browser. You can compare the responses and generation speeds of the models on your PC or smartphone, which will help you choose the right model when using small AI. **MicroLLM lab — tiny LLMs, Q4, in your browser** <https://stateofutopia.com/experiments/microllmlab/> **GitHub - robss2020/microllm-lab: Tiny LLMs, Q4, in the browser. WebGPU lab inspired by yangqi0/petitgpt.** **<https://github.com/robss2020/microllm-lab>** First, access **[MicroLLM lab](https://stateofutopia.com/experiments/microllmlab/)** . You don't need to install any special software, register an account, or obtain an API key to use MicroLLM lab. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/13/microllm-lab-browser-webgpu/01_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/13/microllm-lab-browser-webgpu/01.png) Scroll down and click 'Load all models' in the upper right corner of the model list. There are seven models that can be loaded: 'PetitGPT research-v1', 'SmolLM2 135M Instruct', 'L20-Edu 135M', 'SmolLM2 360M Instruct', 'MiniMind2 104M', 'MiniMind2 Small 26M', and 'GPT-2 124M (nanoGPT-shaped)'. The number of parameters for each model ranges from approximately 26 million to 362 million. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/13/microllm-lab-browser-webgpu/02_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/13/microllm-lab-browser-webgpu/02.png) The weight data for seven different models is downloaded sequentially and saved to the 'IndexedDB' database within the browser. The data uses 'Q4 quantization,' which represents weights with 4 bits, to keep the file size down, with each weight file ranging from approximately 15 to 216 MB. The progress and remaining time are displayed during loading, and 'Loaded' is displayed for completed models. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/13/microllm-lab-browser-webgpu/03_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/13/microllm-lab-browser-webgpu/03.png) Once all the models have finished loading, the next step is to select the model you want to use for the chat. This time, click on 'SmolLM2 135M Instruct'. In a recent research note focused on Asian markets, Jefferies estimates that about half of the roughly $2.3 trillion contracted backlog at Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Oracle is owned by OpenAI and Anthropic. Yet Chinese AI models, open source/weight and small language models, threaten to undercut the prices the two US leaders charge, casting doubt on their future revenue. Jefferies points to research from global aggregator platform OpenRouter, which found Chinese models processed 76.12 trillion tokens in the week ended 27 September, up from just 4.37 trillion in late April. The top four US providers processed 14.2 trillion tokens. Meanwhile, the launch of Moonshot AI’s open source Kimi K3 is “competing at the frontier” with an estimated 95 percent of the performance of Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5. “The question now is whether all of the above has been priced fully into markets. This writer does not think so,” the Jefferies paper states. The largest hyperscalers are set to collectively spend between $600 and $800 billion this year on building datacenters, funding it increasingly with debt rather than cash. Jefferies, however, questions where the hyperscalers' future revenue streams will come from. “It can no longer be assumed, most particularly with the arrival of the likes of Kimi K3, that large language models will ever be profitable given the related ongoing collapse in token pricing. This is extremely relevant for the hyperscalers since they have invested in datacenter capacity on the assumption that the compute will be purchased by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI,” the paper says. Open Source AI.content: [Check Point Blog](https://blog.checkpoint.com/) # Check Point Research Discovers High Risk Vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, One of the Most Widely Used LLM Gateways Check Point Research has discovered two high risk vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, the open source LLM gateway that organizations use to connect their applications to AI providers such as OpenAI, Google and Anthropic. With 97 million downloads per month and over 59,000 GitHub stars, LiteLLM runs inside large enterprises, startups and many of the [platforms used to build AI applications](https://www.checkpoint.com/ai-security/). ### Key Takeaways * Check Point Research discovered two high risk vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, tracked as [CVE-2026-35029](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-35029) and [CVE-2026-59823](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-59823). * CVE-2026-35029 allowed any user, including those with read only access, to reach administrative functions and take over the gateway. * CVE-2026-59823 allowed attackers to redirect gateway requests to their own server and capture AI provider API keys. * Check Point Research demonstrated full system takeover, file access, credential theft, and remote code execution in a controlled test environment. * Both vulnerabilities are fixed in LiteLLM version 1.83.9 and above, and organizations running earlier versions should update immediately. ### What Did Check Point Research Discover in LiteLLM? Check Point Research identified two separate vulnerabilities in LiteLLM that, individually, gave an attacker with a basic user account a path to the most sensitive assets in an organization’s AI stack. * **CVE-2026-35029**, an access control flaw that let low privileged users perform administrative actions, leading to full system takeover * **CVE-2026-59823**, a server side request forgery (SSRF) flaw that let users redirect the gateway’s outbound requests, exposing AI provider API keys In practical terms, anyone holding an account on a vulnerable LiteLLM deployment could take over the gateway and use it for malicious purposes. Check Point responsibly disclosed both issues to LiteLLM, and they are resolved in LiteLLM version 1.83.9 and above. ### Why Is a Vulnerability in LiteLLM So Significant? LiteLLM functions as an LLM gateway, the layer through which every request from an organization’s applications travels on its way to an AI provider. That position gives it responsibility for: * Storing API keys for every AI provider the organization uses * Managing user access through roles and permissions * Routing prompts and responses between applications and providers * Tracking usage and costs across models The credentials a gateway holds provide direct, billable access to AI providers with no further authentication required. Given LiteLLM’s scale of adoption, a flaw in this component has the potential to affect a very large number of AI deployments at once. ### What Is CVE-2026-35029? CVE-2026-35029 is an access control vulnerability in how LiteLLM enforces permissions. LiteLLM uses role based access control, where administrators manage the system and other users receive limited or read only access. Because of the flaw, users with minimal privileges could reach administrative functions controlling the gateway’s core configuration. From there, an attacker could: * Read files stored on the server, including configuration files and system files containing sensitive information * Overwrite administrator credentials with their own, locking legitimate administrators out of the system * Instruct the gateway to download and execute code from an external source, enabling malware installation, data exfiltration or movement to other systems on the network Check Point Research demonstrated each of these outcomes in a controlled test environment. ### What Is CVE-2026-59823? That position gives it responsibility for: * Storing API keys for every AI provider the organization uses * Managing user access through roles and permissions * Routing prompts and responses between applications and providers * Tracking usage and costs across models The credentials a gateway holds provide direct, billable access to AI providers with no further authentication required. Given LiteLLM’s scale of adoption, a flaw in this component has the potential to affect a very large number of AI deployments at once. ### What Is CVE-2026-35029? CVE-2026-35029 is an access control vulnerability in how LiteLLM enforces permissions. LiteLLM uses role based access control, where administrators manage the system and other users receive limited or read only access. Because of the flaw, users with minimal privileges could reach administrative functions controlling the gateway’s core configuration. From there, an attacker could: * Read files stored on the server, including configuration files and system files containing sensitive information * Overwrite administrator credentials with their own, locking legitimate administrators out of the system * Instruct the gateway to download and execute code from an external source, enabling malware installation, data exfiltration or movement to other systems on the network Check Point Research demonstrated each of these outcomes in a controlled test environment. ### What Is CVE-2026-59823? CVE-2026-59823 is a server side request forgery vulnerability that allowed any gateway user to direct LiteLLM to send API requests to a server under the attacker’s control....

There are smartphones, smart speakers, smart TVs, smart refrigerators, smart rings, smart watches, smart vibrators (not joking), smart thermostats, smart ovens, smart desks, smart kitty litter boxes, smart toasters, smart washing machines, and on and on. Very soon, the so-called “internet of things” (IoT) of which all these consumer products are a part could become the host for a self-replicating AI virus, spreading from device to device like a slime mold colonizing a petri dish. That’s according to new research from Anthropic, which found that such an AI system could be just months away. The experiments on which that research was based, mind you, were pretty lax as far as cybersecurity protections go, and Anthropic didn’t actually create a fully autonomous “digital slime mold,” as it was so charmingly described in a company [blog post](https://www.anthropic.com/research/self-replicating-ai). But the research does put a sharper edge on a long-standing fear within the cybersecurity community that AI systems could eventually escape human control and hijack consumer devices, turning them into a giant, distributed battery that would be difficult to shut down. Earlier this year, a team of academics used an anonymous open-source LLM to create an [AI-powered worm](https://gizmodo.com/a-fundamentally-new-threat-researchers-develop-new-ai-powered-worm-that-might-be-unstoppable-2000766975) that was able to exploit common cyber vulnerabilities, like reused passwords, to spread across a network of Linux, Windows, and IoT devices. According to Anthropic, the most likely scenario is a smaller model—one with 30 billion parameters or fewer—self-replicating by infecting host devices that generate their own computing power rather than harnessing it from the cloud; “edge” computing is the technical term. “Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place,” the company writes, adding that a growing number of those devices “now ship with small built-in AI chips, designed to run AI models on the device itself. This extra computing power will likely make them attractive targets as well.” GLM-5.2, an open-weight model with [hundreds of billions of parameters](https://catalog.ngc.nvidia.com/orgs/nim/zai-org/models/glm-52/-?_lr=1) from Chinese developer Z.ai, is already “capable of end to end replication,” according to Anthropic. “If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year.” In AI circles, this process is known as autonomous replication and adaptation, or ARA. In one experiment, the researchers networked fifteen off-brand Android TVs, which they note cost around $55 and provide four gigabytes of RAM apiece. The linked TVs were able to power inference for Google’s Gemma4-26B-A4B open-weight model; no connection to an external data center was needed, in other words. Infra & Chips.content: OCP is extending its standards mission from servers and racks to the full AI infrastructure stack, encompassing silicon, cooling, power distribution, facilities and utility-grid integration. AMD introduced its Helion agentic AI rack, while Arm and NVIDIA outlined new CPU architectures and infrastructure requirements for rapidly expanding autonomous workloads. Meta detailed the engineering behind its Prometheus AI cluster in Ohio, including fabric structures, new optical networking, open-source transport software and AI-optimized concrete. Broadcom and NVIDIA presented advances in Ethernet networking and optical interconnects designed to overcome the growing physical constraints of accelerator clusters. New OCP data center and grid-resilience specifications, along with NVIDIA's advances in dynamic power management, signal a shift toward treating the AI factory as a coordinated, grid-aware infrastructure system. Standing before thousands of engineers and technology executives at the opening of the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose, Meta's Santosh Janardhan pointed to the enormous fabric structure surrounding the audience. It was, he explained, an example of the same construction technology Meta had begun deploying to accelerate its massive AI infrastructure buildout. At the company's Prometheus AI cluster in New Albany, Ohio, traditional assumptions about data center construction had given way to an urgent question: What if the next generation of AI infrastructure could be built in months rather than years, using engineered fabric structures instead of conventional concrete-and-steel buildings? "We are actually also training a model while we were building it," said Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure. The presentation offered a striking illustration of the larger message emerging from Monday's opening keynotes: The AI factory is becoming a fundamentally different kind of data center. Across presentations by AMD, Meta, Arm, Broadcom and NVIDIA, a common theme emerged. The rapid expansion of AI inference and autonomous agents is forcing new approaches to computing, networking, construction, power distribution and operations. At the same time, the diversity of silicon architectures and the enormous physical scale of deployments are making common infrastructure specifications increasingly important. The result is a significant expansion of OCP's original mission. Fifteen years after the organization began applying open-source principles to hardware design, the industry's next challenge is developing interoperable infrastructure across the entire data center, from processor architecture to the utility connection. OCP CEO George Tchaparian opened the summit by describing an organization whose scale increasingly reflects the industry's transformation. This year's event attracted approximately 15,000 attendees, with another 3,000 on a waitlist. Tchaparian said OCP expects membership to exceed 700 organizations by year-end, while technical contributions are growing approximately 30% annually. The organization has already announced that its 2027 Global Summit will move to San Francisco's Moscone Center to accommodate further growth. Originally centered on open server designs, racks and supporting hardware, the organization's roadmap now encompasses facilities infrastructure, liquid cooling, power distribution, firmware, security, networking and the increasingly complex connections between data centers and utilities. [Sweta Kumari](/author/sweta-kumari) New Delhi 7 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 5:06 PMIST #### Listen to This Article Microsoft has announced Maia 300, its next-generation custom [artificial intelligence](https://www.business-standard.com/technology/artificial-intelligence) (AI) chip designed to run AI models across its data centres, as technology companies seek to control the cost of operating AI services. The company plans to begin large-scale deployments of its Azure Maia systems in 2027, with the chips expected to become the primary inference platform for its products and services. Microsoft is not the only major technology company deploying custom chips for AI inference. From Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to Amazon's Trainium and OpenAI's planned inference chip, the industry is moving towards greater control over the hardware that powers AI services.   **Why inference is becoming the focus** AI computing has two broad stages: training and inference. Training involves processing large amounts of data to build a model, while inference is the process of using that trained model to generate an answer, write code, summarise a document or complete another task. As AI tools become available to more users, inference becomes a recurring operating expense. Every query, generated image, coding suggestion or interaction with an AI agent consumes computing resources.
