Infra & Chips.content: UPDATED 10:38 EDT / OCTOBER 13 2026 ### On theCUBE Pod: AI doubters get loud, and IBM seeks competitive advantage by Devony Hof Americans have big concerns about artificial intelligence, but that hasn’t stopped OpenAI Inc., Nvidia Corp., IBM Corp. and others from charging ahead. Last week saw shares of Nvidia, CoreWeave Inc., Oracle Corp. and Nebius Group N.V. decline amid reports that OpenAI’s annualized net revenue was approximately $50 billion, roughly $20 billion below previously reported figures. Despite the ongoing public pushback against AI, John Furrier (pictured, right), research executive analyst at theCUBE Research, sees the uproar as temporary. “This is an AI freakout moment,” he said. “It’s funny to watch knowing what’s happening on the inside. We talk to all those suppliers, whether it’s Nvidia, the chip side … the neoclouds or the AI infrastructure clouds. This new AI layer is a system; the data center as a system is now the computer. Rack scale is changing. Companies like Marvell, Broadcom and others are creating chips to create more efficiencies.” On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, left), chief analyst at theCUBE Research, discussed takeaways from the recent IBM Analyst Council. They also explored chipmaker Marvell Technology Inc.’s growth and the industry shift toward inference. ### IBM bets on commodity models Big Blue’s recent meeting provided insights into the legacy company’s position in the AI era. As Vellante sees it, customers are increasingly spending on the infrastructure and models needed to produce intelligence before turning to IBM to put that intelligence to work, presenting a challenge for the company as the AI market matures. “The alpha is going to be in your data, your processes and your operating model,” Vellante said. “This is [IBM’s] opportunity. That AI operating model is going to be the new source of competitive advantage. It’s not going to come from Palantir; it’s not going to come from models. It’s going to come from your own proprietary data, how you apply that data, how you streamline your processes and how fast you can get products and services to market.” IBM has promoted a four-part architecture composed of agents, data, automation and hybrid infrastructure, with an orchestration layer that can integrate agents from different vendors. Rather than relying exclusively on proprietary models, IBM is positioning itself as a provider of hybrid AI operating infrastructure for enterprise customers, building on Red Hat’s open-source foundation. “Their bet is the commoditization of the models,” Furrier said. “Having a nice model management capability will be good for IBM; but when you have a commoditization bet, you better be right. IBM doesn’t need its own proprietary operating system [because] … they have a valuable abstraction control layer around open infrastructure through Red Hat. Red Hat gets paid a lot of money to manage that open abstraction. That’s an opportunity: IBM could run all the agents.” The question remains whether IBM’s bet on commodity models and open-source solutions will pay off. Customers trust IBM. but they don’t see the company as an innovator in the current AI landscape, according to Vellante. However, if IBM can establish itself as a provider of the operational infrastructure around AI models and agents, then it could own “the scarcity around the abundance.” “They’ve got to play in both camps,” Vellante added. “In other words, they’ve got to have the IBM version of Oracle’s Red Stack. Last year, we asked [IBM’s CCO] Rob Thomas, what is the platform? And the answer came back: Red Hat. I agree. Let’s build a solution around Red Hat to simplify the adoption of AI. It’s unclear to me what that solution is. It’s clear to me they got all the piece parts.” ### AI market enters the inference stage In the chip world, Marvell Technology Inc. is drawing attention with an ambitious revenue target of $70 billion to $90 billion for fiscal ...

Infra & Chips.title: Intel GPU D-series AI inference chip specs revealed at OCP 2026
Infra & Chips.titleZh: Intel GPU D-series AI inference chip specs revealed at OCP 2026
Infra & Chips.content: [![Quartz](https://static.qz.com/quartz-v1.137.0/_next/static/media/quartz-logo.1poxn91047rb6.svg?dpl=1nln7blm5540)](/) [A.I.](/tech-innovation/ai) # Intel is revealing specs for its new GPU D-series AI inference chip at industry summit The chip, formerly code-named Crescent Island, delivers 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute and 480GB of memory within a 350-watt power envelope [By Cris Tolomia](/author/cristolomia)·2 min read·Updated October 13, 2026 [Add QZ to Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=qz.com) Justin Sullivan / Getty Images Intel[$INTC](/quote/INTC) [shared technical details](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/newsroom/news/artificial-intelligence/intel-accelerates-open-infrastructure-agentic-ai-era.html) Monday on its GPU D-series AI inference chip at the Open Compute Project Global Summit, giving the product formerly code-named Crescent Island its official name and disclosing key performance specifications for the first time. According to Intel, the chip is based on the Xe3P architecture and delivers up to 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute alongside 1.5 TB/s of memory bandwidth and as much as 480GB of LPDDR5X memory, all within a 350-watt power envelope. It uses a standard PCIe form factor and air-cooled design, allowing deployment in existing data center environments without specialized rack or cooling infrastructure. Intelsaid the GPU D-series is designed for large language models, long-context workloads and concurrent inference services. A single card can support models with up to 300 billion parameters, while an eight-GPU system can handle models exceeding one trillion parameters, according to the company. "Inference is becoming the defining AI workload, and enterprises need infrastructure that delivers the right performance at the right cost," Anil Nanduri, vice president of AI Products and GTM at Intel's Data Center Group, said in a statement. "With IntelGPU D-series, we're focused on making high-capacity inference practical to deploy and economical to scale." Customer sampling of GPU D-series products is underway, Intelsaid, though the company did not announce a broad launch date or pricing. The GPU D-series targets a different performance and infrastructure profile than Nvidia[$NVDA](/quote/NVDA)'s highest-end hardware, according to [Tom's Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/intels-crescent-island-ai-accelerator-officially-powers-new-gpu-d-series-products-chip-delivers-1-3-peak-pflops-of-fp8-compute-and-1-5-tb-s-of-memory-bandwidth). Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system packs 72 Rubin GPUs, each capable of 17.5 petaflops of FP8 throughput, but the platform demands liquid cooling and draws substantially more power, according to Tom's Hardware. Intelalso introduced new Xeon-based rack designs at the summit. Select Xeon 6+ configurations can scale beyond 46,000 cores per rack at 133.45 kilowatts of total rack power, the company said. Many of the new rack designs use the Open Compute Project's Open Rack v3 standard to simplify deployment in open data center infrastructure. Intelsaid its commercialization efforts involve a range of partners across the supply chain, including OEMs, ODMs, neoclouds, independent software vendors, appliance providers, and AI-native companies. The company also highlighted a contribution to the OCP's Open Adapter Card workgroup, which is working to define a standardized sub-rack accelerator card form factor to improve interoperability across system designs. Intelhas made 116 contributions to the Open Compute Project since 2011, the company said. Daily Brief ## The essential business news, delivered fresh every morning. Infra & Chips.content: ## Since 1987: Covering the Fastest Computers in the World and the People Who Run Them ### TCI Media: Home of the Wire Publications ![Header Logo 1](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/ai-600-300x73-1.webp) ![Header Logo 2](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/data-600-300x72-1.webp) ![Header Logo 3](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/qc-600-300x69-1.webp) ![Logo](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/hpc-logo-300x60-1.jpg) ## Off the Wire Press Releases ### October 13, 2026 ### October 12, 2026 ## NVIDIA Details Open Designs for AI Power, Cooling and Networking Oct. 13, 2026 — As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/) announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/nvidia-shutterstock_2705357347-300x225.jpg) Credit: Robert Way/Shutterstock NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. **NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances** At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The [news at OCP](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/ocp-summit/) spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance. **Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP** NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. Infra & Chips.content: ![Download Indmoney App QR Code](https://ast.indmoneycdn.com/cdn-cgi/image/quality=90,format=auto,width=72/https://ast.indmoneycdn.com/cdn/qr_icon_blue.png "Download Indmoney App QR Code") # Microsoft Maia 300 vs Nvidia: Can Microsoft Disrupt the AI Chip Market in 2027? ![Kashish Jindal Image](https://ast.indmoneycdn.com/strapiauthor/kashish-jindal.png "Kashish Jindal Image") [Kashish Jindal](/blog/author/kashish-jindal) Last updated: 12 min read ![Microsoft vs Nvidia: AI Chip Battle](https://strapi-cdn.indmoney.com/cdn-cgi/image/quality=80,format=auto,metadata=copyright,width=700/https://strapi-cdn.indmoney.com/xlarge_Microsoft_vs_Nvidia_AI_Chip_Battle_d2e5ec0947.png "Microsoft vs Nvidia: AI Chip Battle") Table Of Contents * What is Microsoft Maia 300 and when will it launch? * Why Microsoft wants to control more of its AI costs * How Maia 300’s design could improve AI inference * Does 40% more tokens per megawatt mean 40% lower costs? * Can Maia 300 compete with Nvidia’s AI platform? * What could Maia 300 mean for Microsoft’s valuation? * How Maia could affect Nvidia’s revenue and margins * What Indian investors should watch before the 2027 rollout * Can Microsoft challenge Nvidia in 2027? The investor verdict Microsoft’s Maia 300 announcement brings an uncomfortable question for Nvidia: what happens when a major customer starts producing more of its own AI computing? Scheduled for production deployment in 2027, the chip could strengthen Microsoft’s economics. But challenging Nvidia inside Microsoft’s services is a different task from replacing it across the AI industry. Let’s break down what Maia 300 does, how its performance claims translate into financial value and what investors should watch before declaring a winner. ## **What is Microsoft Maia 300 and when will it launch?** Maia 300 is Microsoft’s third-generation custom AI accelerator. Microsoft announced it on October 12 and plans to make the Maia family its primary inference system for its own products and services through multi-gigawatt deployments beginning in 2027. Inference means using a trained model to produce an answer or perform a task. Training builds the model’s capabilities. Inference puts those capabilities to work whenever someone asks an AI assistant to summarise a document, generate code or analyse information. | | | | --- | --- | | **Announcement detail** | **What Microsoft disclosed** | | **Announcement date** | October 12, 2026 | | **Production deployment** | Begins in 2027 | | **Main target** | AI inference | | **Intended role** | Primary inference system for Microsoft’s own products and services | | **Existing foundation** | Maia 200 already serves production workloads including Microsoft Copilot | *Sources: Microsoft’s October 12 Maia announcement; Microsoft Azure’s Maia 300 architecture disclosure.* The important word is “own”.
